title: Reading Apocalyptic
summary: Daniel and Revelation in the family of ancient Jewish and Christian apocalypses: what the genre is, how its visions, symbols, and numbers work, the debates over dating, and the four main schools of interpreting Revelation (preterist, historicist, futurist, and idealist) with their history.

sections.body:
The word apocalypse comes from the Greek apokalypsis, ‘unveiling’ or ‘revelation’, the first word of the book of Revelation: “This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass.” (Revelation 1:1). In ordinary speech ‘apocalypse’ has come to mean catastrophe, the end of the world. In the Bible it means something different: the drawing back of a curtain so that a human being is shown what is normally hidden, the reality of heaven and the true meaning and direction of history.

Scholars use the word for a whole family of ancient Jewish and Christian writings from roughly 250 BC to AD 250. In 1979 a working group of the Society of Biblical Literature led by John J. Collins published a definition in the journal Semeia (volume 14) that has become standard. In summary, an apocalypse is a kind of revelatory writing with a narrative frame, in which a revelation is given to a human recipient through an otherworldly figure, usually an angel, disclosing a reality that is both temporal, because it looks toward final salvation and judgment, and spatial, because it involves another, supernatural world. Collins developed the picture further in The Apocalyptic Imagination (first edition 1984).

The Bible contains two books usually classed as apocalypses, Daniel (in its second half, chapters 7 to 12) and Revelation. Apocalyptic features also appear in other passages: Isaiah 24 to 27 (often called the Isaiah Apocalypse), Ezekiel 38 and 39, Zechariah's night visions (Zechariah 1 to 6) and his final chapters, parts of Joel, Jesus' discourse on the end in Mark 13 (with Matthew 24 and Luke 21, sometimes called the Little Apocalypse), and Paul's teaching in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 2 Thessalonians 2. Many scholars see apocalyptic as growing out of prophecy, especially the visionary prophecy of Ezekiel and Zechariah, in a time when Israel lived under foreign empires and asked where God's kingdom was.

It helps to distinguish three things that are often blurred: the apocalypse as a kind of book; apocalyptic eschatology, a set of convictions about the end (two ages, a coming judgment, resurrection, cosmic renewal); and apocalypticism, the outlook of a community shaped by those convictions. The Dead Sea Scrolls community at Qumran is an example of the last: its War Scroll pictures a final battle between the sons of light and the sons of darkness.

Daniel and Revelation have many relatives outside the Bible, and reading a few of them (or about them) makes the biblical books far less strange. The oldest are the sections of 1 Enoch, a collection attributed to Enoch, the man who ‘walked with God’ in Genesis 5. Its earliest part, the Book of the Watchers, dates from the third century BC and describes the fall of angels and Enoch's tours of heaven and the places of judgment; fragments of it in Aramaic were found at Qumran. The Letter of Jude quotes a line from 1 Enoch (Jude 14-15), and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church includes the whole book in its Bible.

After the destruction of the temple in AD 70, Jewish writers wrestled with the catastrophe through apocalypses. 4 Ezra (chapters 3 to 14 of the book called 2 Esdras in the Apocrypha), written about AD 100, sets a series of anguished dialogues with an angel in the time after Babylon destroyed the first temple, but its real subject is Rome and the second. 2 Baruch, from about the same period, does something similar. Early Christians also wrote apocalypses: the Shepherd of Hermas and the Apocalypse of Peter (both second century) were read in some churches, and the Apocalypse of Peter appears in the Muratorian list of books, with a note that some would not have it read in church.

These works share recognizable features. A seer receives visions, often in dreams or after prayer and fasting, and an angel interprets them. History is divided into periods (four kingdoms, seventy weeks of years, ten weeks), showing that God has ordered it and that the end is set. The world is seen as a battlefield between God and evil powers, heavenly and earthly. Symbols, especially beasts, horns, and numbers, stand for kingdoms and rulers. The suffering of the faithful is placed within God's plan, and a final judgment and resurrection bring justice. Most Jewish apocalypses are also pseudonymous, written in the name of an ancient hero such as Enoch, Abraham, Ezra, or Baruch, and they often present past history as though it were prophecy spoken long before.

Revelation both belongs to this family and stands out from it. Its author is not an ancient hero but a contemporary, John, who names himself as “your brother and partner in the tribulation” (Revelation 1:9), writing to seven real churches in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey). It calls itself a prophecy (1:3) and is framed as a letter (1:4 and 22:21). It is meant to be read aloud and understood, not sealed: “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near.” (22:10), in deliberate contrast to Daniel, who was told to “shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4). Richard Bauckham (The Theology of the Book of Revelation and The Climax of Prophecy, both 1993) has shown how Revelation takes up and transforms the apocalyptic tradition around the figure of the slain Lamb.

sections.h: Daniel: stories, visions, and the dating debate
sections.body:
Daniel has two halves. Chapters 1 to 6 are stories about Daniel and his three friends as Jewish exiles serving in the courts of Babylon and Persia: the refusal of the king's food, Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a statue, the fiery furnace, the king's madness, the writing on the wall, and the lions' den. Chapters 7 to 12 are Daniel's own visions, told in the first person. The book is also bilingual: it begins in Hebrew, switches to Aramaic at 2:4 when the Babylonian astrologers speak to the king, stays in Aramaic through chapter 7, and returns to Hebrew for chapters 8 to 12. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include additions preserved in Greek: the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men (in chapter 3), and the stories of Susanna and of Bel and the Dragon.

The visions use symbolic beasts for empires. In Daniel 7, four beasts rise from the churning sea, and the angel explains, “These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth.” (7:17). Then “One like the Son of Man” comes “with the clouds of heaven” to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom (7:13-14). This figure became Jesus' favorite way of referring to himself, and at his trial he applied the verse to himself (Mark 14:62). Daniel 8 identifies some of its beasts outright: the ram is Media and Persia, and “The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece” (8:21), meaning Alexander the Great, whose empire split into four.

When was Daniel written? Jewish and Christian tradition held that Daniel wrote it in the sixth century BC, and many conservative scholars defend that view, among them E. J. Young (The Prophecy of Daniel, 1949), Joyce Baldwin (Daniel, Tyndale, 1978), and Stephen Miller (New American Commentary, 1994). They point to the book's own claims, to Jesus' reference to ‘the prophet Daniel’ (Matthew 24:15), to details of the Babylonian and Persian court they regard as accurate, and to the conviction that God can reveal the future. The pagan philosopher Porphyry, in the third century AD, argued instead that Daniel was written during the persecution of the Jews by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 to 164 BC), because the visions of chapters 8 and 11 describe that king's reign in precise detail and then become vague; Jerome's commentary on Daniel (about 407) preserves Porphyry's argument in order to answer it. Most modern critical scholars, such as John J. Collins (Hermeneia, 1993), date the visions to about 167 to 164 BC, after Antiochus desecrated the temple and before his death, with the court stories older. They read the ‘abomination of desolation’ (Daniel 11:31) as Antiochus's pagan altar set up in the temple in 167 BC, an event recorded in 1 Maccabees 1:54. Some scholars take mediating positions, for instance older material shaped in its final form later. Copies of Daniel were found at Qumran, at least one probably from the late second century BC, which shows the book was already valued within a generation or two of the critical date.

The four kingdoms of Daniel 2 and 7 are also read two ways. The traditional Christian reading, found in Jerome and followed by many conservatives, identifies them as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome, so that God's kingdom arrives in the Roman period with Christ. The critical reading takes them as Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece, with the little horn of chapter 7 as Antiochus IV. The seventy weeks of Daniel 9:24-27 have produced a still wider range of interpretations: calculations that run to the ministry and death of Christ (the nineteenth-century British writer Sir Robert Anderson's The Coming Prince, 1881, is a famous example), the dispensational view that places a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks, which is then still future, and the critical view that ends the weeks with Antiochus, identifying the anointed one who is cut off (9:26) with the high priest Onias III, murdered about 171 BC. Jesus' own use of Daniel's language for the coming destruction of the temple (Mark 13:14, “when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be (let the reader understand)”) shows that the early church read Daniel's visions as still open to further fulfillment.

The first rule for reading Daniel and Revelation is that the visions are symbolic, and their symbols are drawn from somewhere. The books themselves often say so. Revelation explains its own opening image: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.” (Revelation 1:20). Later the angel explains that the seven heads of the beast “are seven mountains on which the woman sits” (17:9), and that the woman “is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth” (17:18), which the first readers would have understood as Rome, the city built on seven hills. When the text gives an interpretation, the reader should take it; when it does not, the reader should look first to where the symbol came from.

For Revelation, the main source is the Old Testament. The book never formally quotes it, but alludes to it constantly, scholars count several hundred allusions, especially to Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Zechariah, Exodus, and the Psalms. The beast from the sea in Revelation 13 combines the features of Daniel's four beasts into one. The plagues of the trumpets and bowls echo the plagues of Egypt. The new Jerusalem echoes Ezekiel's temple vision and Isaiah's new heavens and new earth. The second source is the world of the first readers: the imperial cult, emperors who claimed divine titles, the trade that flowed to Rome, and the pressure on Christians in cities such as Pergamum and Smyrna.

Revelation often uses a pattern in which John hears one thing and then sees another, and the second image interprets the first. In chapter 5 John hears of “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” who has triumphed, and he turns and sees “a Lamb who appeared to have been slain” (5:5-6). The conquering Messiah conquers by being slain. In chapter 7 John hears the number of the sealed, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel (7:4), and then sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” (7:9). Many interpreters, Bauckham among them, read these as two views of the same people of God, first as Israel's army counted for battle, then as the fulfillment of the promise to Abraham of countless descendants from all nations. Other interpreters, especially dispensationalists, take the 144,000 as a distinct group of Jewish believers.

The visions also repeat. Revelation's series of sevens, the seven seals, seven trumpets, and seven bowls, can be read as successive events or as overlapping views of the same period, each intensifying toward the end. The idea that the series recapitulate, or retell the same story from different angles, goes back to Victorinus of Pettau (died about 304), whose commentary is the oldest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation. William Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors (1939) developed it into a scheme of seven parallel sections.

Numbers in apocalyptic writing are mostly symbols of quality rather than quantities to be calculated. Seven stands for completeness, drawing on the seven days of creation; Revelation is built of sevens and speaks of “the seven Spirits” before God's throne (1:4), a way of speaking of the Holy Spirit in his fullness. Twelve is the number of God's people, the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, and its multiples (twenty-four elders, 144,000, the city of twelve thousand stadia) express the whole people of God. Four is the number of the world, with its four corners and four winds. A thousand is a large, complete number. Ten can stand for a limited fullness, as in the ‘ten days’ of tribulation promised to the church at Smyrna (2:10).

One period recurs in several forms: forty-two months (11:2), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14), which is three and a half years. The phrase comes from Daniel (7:25 and 12:7), and three and a half is half of seven: a time of trouble that is real but broken off, limited by God. The same period appears in Revelation for the trampling of the holy city, the witness of the two witnesses, and the woman's protection in the wilderness, which suggests that all three are ways of describing the same season of the church's life under pressure.

The most famous number is 666, “the number of a man” (13:18). In the ancient world letters served as numbers, and adding up the letters of a name was a common game, known in Greek as isopsephy and in Hebrew as gematria. The best-known solution is that the letters of ‘Nero Caesar’ written in Hebrew add to 666. Some ancient manuscripts, including a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (P115, from the third century) and the fifth-century Codex Ephraemi, read 616 instead, which is the value of the same name in the Latin spelling without the final n; Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30) knew the 616 reading and rejected it. Many scholars take the Nero solution as correct, often connecting it with the widespread legend that Nero would return. Others think 666 is primarily symbolic, falling short of seven three times over. Revelation calls the calculation “a call for wisdom”, and its point for the first readers seems to be that the beast is a human power, not a god, however much it demands worship.

The long history of attempts to calculate the date of the end from these numbers is a warning. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.” (Matthew 24:36), and every date set by calculation has passed.

Revelation was written by a man named John while he was on the island of Patmos, off the coast of Asia Minor, “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9), probably a form of banishment. Early tradition, from Justin Martyr in the second century, identified him with John the apostle. In the third century Dionysius of Alexandria, comparing the Greek style of Revelation with the Gospel of John, argued that the two could not be by the same writer, and many modern scholars agree, speaking of John the prophet or John the seer; others maintain apostolic authorship. The seven churches addressed in chapters 2 and 3 are real congregations in cities of the Roman province of Asia, Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea, and the letters to them are full of local detail.

There are two main views of the date. Irenaeus, writing about AD 180 (Against Heresies 5.30.3), said the vision was seen toward the end of the reign of the emperor Domitian, who ruled from AD 81 to 96, and most scholars accept a date of about AD 95. Others argue for a date in the late 60s, under or just after Nero (who ruled 54 to 68 and persecuted Christians in Rome after the fire of 64), before the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. This view was held by several nineteenth-century scholars, including B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, and has been argued in more recent times by John A. T. Robinson (Redating the New Testament, 1976) and Kenneth Gentry (Before Jerusalem Fell, 1989). The date matters especially for preterist interpretation, since an early date allows Revelation to be read as foretelling the fall of Jerusalem.

Either way, the first readers lived under Roman power and the religion of the empire, in which the emperor was honored with temples, statues, and sacrifices, and in which a Christian's refusal to take part could cost a trade, a place in society, or a life. One church member in Pergamum, Antipas, had already been killed (2:13). Revelation's pictures of a beast demanding worship, a mark required to buy and sell, and a prostitute city drunk on the blood of the saints were written into that world. The book's message to those churches is to hold fast: “Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” (2:10).

Christians have read Revelation in four main ways, usually called the preterist, historicist, futurist, and idealist schools. They differ mainly on when the events of chapters 4 to 22 take place. Each has a long history, and each has been held by serious and faithful interpreters. Most modern commentators combine elements of more than one.

The preterist view (from the Latin praeter, ‘past’) holds that most of Revelation's prophecies were fulfilled in the first centuries: in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or in God's judgment on persecuting Rome, or both. Revelation, on this view, addressed its first readers about events that were about to happen, as its repeated ‘soon’ and ‘the time is near’ suggest (1:1, 3; 22:10). The first systematic preterist commentary was written by the Spanish Jesuit Luis de Alcázar (1554 to 1613), published after his death in 1614, partly to counter the Protestant identification of the pope with the Antichrist. Most academic commentaries today read Revelation primarily against its first-century Roman setting. Partial preterists, such as Kenneth Gentry and R. C. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus, 1998), hold that many prophecies were fulfilled in AD 70 while the return of Christ, the resurrection, and the final judgment remain future. A minority position, full preterism (argued, for example, by J. Stuart Russell in The Parousia, 1878), holds that the second coming and the resurrection were also fulfilled in AD 70; nearly all churches reject this because the creeds confess a future return of Christ and bodily resurrection.

The historicist view reads Revelation as a prophetic outline of the whole history of the church, from John's day to the end, with the seals, trumpets, and bowls matching successive events in European history. It often uses a year-for-a-day principle, so that 1,260 days become 1,260 years. Its roots lie in the medieval abbot Joachim of Fiore (died 1202), who read history in three ages, and it became the dominant Protestant reading from the Reformation to the nineteenth century: Luther, in his preface to Revelation of 1530, read the book as a picture of church history, and many Reformers and Puritans identified the papacy with the Antichrist, as the Westminster Confession of 1646 did (25.6). Isaac Newton's Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John (published 1733) and E. B. Elliott's four-volume Horae Apocalypticae (1844) are classic historicist works. William Miller's historicist calculations led thousands of Americans to expect Christ's return in 1844, and the Seventh-day Adventist Church, which grew out of that movement, still holds the historicist view. Critics note that historicist interpreters have tended to find the climax of the book in their own age, and that the scheme makes much of Revelation unintelligible to its first readers.

The futurist view holds that, after the letters to the seven churches, most of Revelation (chapters 4 to 22) describes events still to come, in a period of tribulation just before the return of Christ. Early church writers such as Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Hippolytus expected a future Antichrist and a future kingdom, and in that sense were futurists. The modern futurist school is often traced to another Spanish Jesuit, Francisco Ribera (1537 to 1591), whose commentary of about 1590 placed most of the book in the last days, again partly as an answer to the Protestant reading. In the nineteenth century, John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren joined futurism to dispensational premillennialism, with a rapture of the church before the tribulation. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909), Dallas Theological Seminary, John Walvoord's commentary (1966), Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), and the Left Behind novels (from 1995) carried this form to a vast audience. Other futurists are not dispensational: George Eldon Ladd (A Commentary on the Revelation of John, 1972) and Robert Mounce (1977) held a historic premillennial futurism without a pretribulation rapture. Critics object that futurism makes most of the book irrelevant to the seven churches to which it was sent.

The idealist view, sometimes called the spiritual or symbolic view, holds that Revelation does not map specific events but portrays in symbols the timeless conflict between God and evil, the church and the world, which is repeated in every age until Christ returns and ends it. Its roots are in the African theologian Tyconius, whose commentary on Revelation (late fourth century, now lost but used by many later writers) read the book spiritually, and in Augustine, who in book 20 of The City of God read the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the present age of the church. This reading dominated the medieval West. Modern idealist or largely idealist commentaries include William Milligan's (1889), Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors (1939), and Michael Wilcock's I Saw Heaven Opened (1975). Critics argue that pure idealism cuts the book loose from its first-century setting and from the real future consummation it announces.

Many recent commentators combine these approaches. G. K. Beale (New International Greek Testament Commentary, 1999) describes his view as a redemptive-historical form of modified idealism, and Grant Osborne (Baker Exegetical Commentary, 2002) calls his eclectic. Such readings take the book as addressed first to the seven churches under Rome, as disclosing patterns that recur throughout the church's history, and as looking forward to a real, future return of Christ, final judgment, and new creation.

sections.body:
Revelation 20 describes Satan bound for a thousand years while those who had been faithful to death “came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years” (20:4). The passage is the only place in the Bible that mentions a millennium, and Christians have held three main views of it. The question is second-order: it has never divided the church's creeds, and faithful Christians hold each view.

Premillennialists hold that Christ will return before (pre-) a literal or at least future reign of Christ on earth, after which comes the final judgment and new creation. Many second-century writers held this, among them Papias, Justin Martyr (who also noted that some orthodox Christians disagreed), and Irenaeus. Modern premillennialism takes two forms: historic premillennialism (Ladd) and dispensational premillennialism (Darby, Scofield, Walvoord), which also distinguishes Israel and the church and usually expects a rapture before the tribulation.

Amillennialists hold that the thousand years is a symbol for the present age between Christ's first and second comings, in which Satan is restrained so that the gospel reaches the nations and the faithful dead reign with Christ in heaven. This view, shaped by Tyconius and Augustine, has been the majority position of the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed traditions.

Postmillennialists hold that Christ will return after (post-) a long period in which the gospel spreads and the world is largely brought to faith and justice. It was widely held among Protestants in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, by Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, and B. B. Warfield among others, and fueled much of the missionary movement of that era.

All three views agree on what the creeds confess: that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, that the dead will be raised, and that God will make all things new. Revelation's last chapters describe that hope in images of a new heaven and earth, a city that needs no temple because “the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (21:22), and a God who will “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (21:4).

A few principles hold across the schools. Read the books as their first hearers would have heard them, as messages to people under pressure from empires, who needed to know that God, not the beast, rules history. Daniel's stories and visions tell exiles and later persecuted Jews that the kingdoms of the world rise and fall while “the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44). Revelation tells seven small churches that the Lamb who was slain, not Caesar, sits at the center of the throne.

Let the books interpret their own symbols where they do, and look to the Old Testament for the rest. Treat numbers as symbols first. Notice the structure, especially the series of sevens and the hear-and-see pairs. Pay attention to the worship scenes, which are the heart of Revelation: the throne room of chapters 4 and 5, the hymns of the redeemed, and the songs that later generations have set to music, such as the texts from Revelation 11:15 and 19:6 and 16 that Handel used for the Hallelujah chorus in Messiah (1742).

Be humble about specific identifications. The history of interpretation is full of confident readings that tied a beast or a horn to a pope, a sultan, an emperor, or a modern dictator, and every generation of such readers has been succeeded by another. Be careful, too, about fear. The books were written to give endurance and hope to people who were suffering, not to frighten the comfortable or feed speculation. Revelation begins with a blessing on those who read it aloud and keep it (1:3), and it ends with a prayer: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (22:20).
